title: Chapter 14: Comprehensions: Transforming Data in One Line
video_title: Python Chapter 14: Comprehensions, Transforming Data in One Line
summary: Asha writes the same three-line loop again and again. Follow her as she learns comprehensions: the same list in one line, text changes, filters, choosing a value with if and else, dictionary comprehensions, and when a normal loop is clearer. Then watch her rewrite a loop with an AI assistant at all six stages. She keeps a checklist, runs every case, and catches a missing filter and curly brackets that made a set.

scenes.direction: Open on the three-line loop pattern that builds a new list, in Asha's words. Then the title with the AI tease, then the menu board as the mission, with no output yet.

visual.heading: Three lines, again and again

Then names in capitals. Then only the vegan items. Asha thinks: another empty list, another loop, another append. There must be a shorter way!

segments.say: So here is today's mission: the menu board for the Corner Cafe. Lines 2 to 5 hold each item, its price, and whether it is vegan.
Lines 6, 7 and 8 are three comprehensions. Each one builds something new in one line.
And the printing stays in a normal loop. You will see why. Let's build it.

scenes.title: Why this matters

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A **comprehension** builds a new list or dictionary from another collection, in one line.
It says what you want, not how to collect it step by step.
Data tools and reports use them to clean and reshape data.
It does not replace every loop. Part of the skill is choosing.

segments.say: A comprehension builds a new list or dictionary from another collection, in one line. It says what you want, not how to collect it.
Data tools and reports use comprehensions all the time. But they do not replace every loop. Part of this chapter is learning to choose.

scenes.title: The idea: three parts in square brackets
scenes.direction: Teach the three parts with the diagram, then the recipe-card comparison and where it stops working. Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Three parts in square brackets
visual.label: The idea
body: Read the middle part first, then the left part. The filter on the right is optional.
visual.pre:
[ round(price * 1.1, 2)   for price in prices    if price < 4 ]
    |                       |                      |
    the new value           the loop               a filter (optional)
    made for each item      same as a for loop     keep it only if True

segments.say: A list comprehension has three parts inside square brackets. Start in the middle: the loop. For price in prices, exactly like a for loop.
On the left is the new value, made for each item. Here, the price with tax, rounded to two places.
And on the right, an optional filter. Keep the item only if the condition is True. No empty list. No append.

visual.heading: A recipe card for a new list
visual.label: Analogy
items: "For each price, if it is under 4, write down the price with tax."
Unlike a real recipe card, it cannot do other jobs on the way.
No printing, and no running total. Only one new list.

segments.say: Think of a comprehension as a recipe card for a new list. For each price, if it is under 4, write down the price with tax.
Unlike a real recipe card, it cannot do other jobs on the way. No printing, and no running total. It only builds the new list.

visual.question: In `[name.upper() for name in items]`, which part is the new value?
visual.explain: The new value comes first, on the left. It is made once for each item.

segments.say: Quick check. In this comprehension, which part is the new value?

after.say: C. Name dot upper. The new value comes first, on the left, and it is made for each item.

items: The new value comes first.
Then the loop.
Then an optional filter.

segments.say: Take a breather. Here is what you know so far. Next, Asha rewrites her tax loop in one line.

scenes.title: Steps 1 and 2: The same list in one line
scenes.direction: Recall the loop from the opening as the known starting point, then the comprehension. Ask what lines 4 and 5 print, then compare.

visual.heading: Steps 1 and 2: The loop, in one line
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 1 is the loop you saw at the start: an empty list, a loop, and append, with round to two places, from Chapter 2.
Step 2. Line 3 builds the same list in one line. The new value first, then for price in prices.
Line 4 prints the new list. Line 5 prints the length of the new list, and the length of the old one.

after.say: Line 4 prints exactly the same list as the loop: 3.85, 4.4, 4.68, and 3.03.
And line 5 prints 4 and 4. Without a filter, the new list has one item for each old item.

scenes.title: Step 3: Transform text
scenes.direction: Teach that the new value can be any expression. Ask what lines 5 and 6 print. Reveal that the old list did not change.

visual.heading: Step 3: Names in title case
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 3. The new value can be any expression. Line 2 holds the menu names, all in small letters.
Line 3 uses title, the string method from Chapter 3. Line 4 uses len, so each new item is a number.

after.say: Line 5 prints the names with capital letters: Tea, Coffee, Carrot Cake, Scone.
Line 6 prints the lengths: 3, 6, 11 and 5. The space in carrot cake counts too.
And line 7 shows the old list, unchanged. A comprehension always makes a new list.

scenes.title: Step 4: Keep only some items
scenes.direction: Teach the filter and unpacking tuples in the loop part, with line 6. Ask what line 9 prints.

visual.heading: Step 4: A filter at the end
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 4. Each tuple holds a name, a price, and whether the item is vegan. The loop part unpacks all three, as in Chapter 13.
An if at the end is a filter. An item goes into the new list only when the condition is True. Line 6 keeps the vegan names.
Line 7 keeps the names of the items that cost less than 4.

after.say: Tea and Scone. Coffee costs exactly 4, and 4 is not less than 4.
And line 8 prints the vegan names: Tea and Coffee. With a filter, the new list can be shorter.

scenes.title: Step 5: Filter or choose
scenes.direction: Contrast the filter at the end with if-else at the start. Ask how many items line 6 prints. Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Step 5: Filter, or choose a value
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 5. Line 3 has an if at the end, so it filters. Only prices under 4 stay.
Line 4 is different. The if and else come first, before the for. That chooses a value for every item: snack under 4, otherwise treat.
This form must have an else, because every item needs a value.

ask.question: How many labels does line 6 print?

after.say: Four. One label for each price: snack, treat, treat, snack.
But line 5 prints only two prices. The filter made that list shorter.

visual.question: Which comprehension keeps only the prices under 4?
options: `[p if p < 4 else 0 for p in prices]`
`[p for p in prices if p < 4]`
visual.explain: A filter goes at the end. The first option keeps every item and swaps some for 0.

segments.say: Quick check. Which comprehension keeps only the prices under 4?

after.say: B. The filter goes at the end. Option A keeps every item, and puts 0 in place of the others.

items: The new value can be any expression.
An `if` at the end filters.
`if ... else` at the start chooses.

segments.say: Breather. Relax for a moment. Next, the same idea builds a whole dictionary.

scenes.title: Step 6: Build a dictionary
scenes.direction: Teach key: value in curly brackets with items() from Chapter 12. Ask what lines 5 and 6 print.

visual.heading: Step 6: A dictionary comprehension
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Step 6. Line 2 is the menu dictionary from Chapter 12.
Line 3 uses curly brackets with a key, a colon, and a value. That makes a dictionary comprehension. Items gives each name and price.
Line 5 reads cake from the new dictionary. Line 6 reads cake from the old menu.

after.say: 4.68, the cake with tax, and then 4.25. The old menu did not change.
Line 4 shows the whole new dictionary: the same keys, with new values.

scenes.title: Step 7: When a loop is clearer
scenes.direction: Show a loop with four jobs per item. Explain why a comprehension would be harder to read here.

visual.heading: Step 7: Four jobs for each item

segments.say: Step 7. Today, items of 4 or more cost 0.50 less, and they get a label. Lines 5 to 7 do that.
Line 8 prints each item, and line 9 adds it to a total. That is four jobs for each item.
A comprehension builds one new list and nothing else. Here, a normal loop is much easier to read.
So the rule is simple. One new list or dictionary: use a comprehension. Several steps, a print, or a running total: use a loop.

scenes.title: See the outcome: the menu board
scenes.direction: Return to the mission. Walk every line, ask what line 12 prints, then reveal. Hand over to the AI feature.

visual.heading: Mission complete: the menu board
visual.hidden_text: Predict the board before it appears.

segments.say: Back to the mission. Line 6 builds a dictionary: each name, with its price plus tax.
Line 7 filters the vegan names. Line 8 filters the board, so it compares the prices with tax.
Lines 9 and 10 print the board with a normal loop, because printing is not building a list.
Line 12 prints the names whose price with tax is under 4.

after.say: Tea and Scone. With tax, Tea is 3.85 and Scone is 3.03. Coffee becomes 4.40, so it is out.
Line 11 prints the vegan items, Tea and Coffee. Three comprehensions, one loop. Mission complete!
Next, Asha wants a loop of her own in one line. She asks an AI assistant, one stage at a time.

scenes.title: Work with AI: six stages, one rewrite
scenes.direction: Teach the refactoring skill. One conversation per stage, all about rewriting the vegan-tax loop. Generate: the AI drops the filter. Test: two cases fail. Debug: if before for, then every case again. Improve: curly brackets fail every case.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: safe refactoring
visual.label: Before you start
items: To **refactor** is to change how code is written, not what it does.
Prove it: run both versions on the same data and compare every line.
Never paste private data. You are responsible for the code you use.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill is safe refactoring. To refactor means to change how code is written, without changing what it does.
And you prove it: run both versions on the same data, and compare every line.

visual.heading: Plan: what must stay the same?

messages.text: I want to rewrite this loop as one line. Do not write code yet. List what the new line must keep exactly the same.

1. Only vegan items: the `if` on line 8.
2. The same order as the menu.
3. Rounding to two decimal places.
4. The result is a list.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha's loop adds tax to the vegan items only. Before any rewrite, she asks the AI what the new line must keep exactly the same.
The AI gives a checklist: only vegan items, the same order, the same rounding, and a list. Asha keeps this checklist.

visual.heading: Write: predict, then run

messages.text: I wrote this loop myself. Do not change it and do not run it. Predict its exact output.

It prints `[3.85, 4.4]`.
Line 8 keeps only Tea and Coffee, and line 9 adds tax and rounds each price.
My prediction was the same. I ran it:

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha wrote the loop herself. She asks the AI to predict its exact output, without running it.
The AI predicts 3.85 and 4.4, only Tea and Coffee. Asha predicted the same, and the run agrees.

visual.heading: Generate: the loop in one line

messages.text: Rewrite my loop as a list comprehension. Keep the output exactly the same, and tell me what it prints.
Here is the one line. It prints `[3.85, 4.4]`, the same as your loop.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks the AI to rewrite her loop as a list comprehension, keep the output the same, and say what it prints.
The AI gives one line, and promises 3.85 and 4.4, the same as the loop.

visual.heading: The AI's line, before Asha runs it
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Here is the AI's line, on line 6. Compare it with the checklist from stage 1.

ask.question: The AI promises `[3.85, 4.4]`. Is it right?

after.say: No. Point 1 on the checklist was the filter. Line 6 has no if at the end, so it keeps every item.
Asha runs it: four prices instead of two. The cake and the scone got tax too. The AI sounded sure, and it dropped part of her loop.

visual.heading: Test: three cases with expected results

messages.text: Give me three test cases with the expected result for each. Use a normal menu and a menu with no vegan items. In the third, two vegan items have the same price.

1. Normal: Tea and Scone. Expected `[3.85]`.
2. No vegan: only Scone. Expected `[]`.
3. Same price: Tea and Mint, both 3.5. Expected `[3.85, 3.85]`.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha asks for three test cases, with the expected result for each.
A normal menu, a menu with no vegan items, and two vegan items with the same price.

visual.heading: Her loop against the AI's line
visual.hidden_text: Predict the results before they appear.

segments.say: Lines 2 to 6 keep the three cases in a dictionary: a name, and a small menu for each.
For each case, lines 8 to 11 run Asha's loop.
Line 12 runs the AI's line. Line 13 uses the same if and else from step 5: it prints pass when both lists are the same, otherwise FAIL.

ask.question: Which cases will the AI's line fail?

after.say: The normal menu and the menu with no vegan items. Both get a scone price they should not have.
The same-price case passes, because both items are vegan. One passing case proves nothing. Run them all.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: I added the filter myself, but the program stops with this error. First explain the cause. Then show the smallest fix.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha tries to add the filter herself, and puts the if before the for. Python stops with a syntax error. She pastes the line and the full error report.

visual.heading: Debug: the AI's answer

messages.text: I added the filter myself, but the program stops with this error. First explain the cause. Then show the smallest fix.

An `if` before the `for` chooses a value for every item, so it needs an `else`.
To keep only some items, move `if vegan` to the end, after `in menu`.

segments.say: The AI explains: an if before the for chooses a value for every item, so it needs an else. Remember step 5. To filter, move if vegan to the end.

visual.heading: Run every case again

segments.say: Asha moves the if to the end, on line 12. Then she runs every case again, because a fix can break a case that worked before.
Normal: 3.85, pass. No vegan: an empty list, pass. Same price: pass. All three cases pass.

visual.heading: Improve: better, but the same?

messages.text: My line passes every case. Suggest one change that makes it better, with one reason. The output must stay exactly the same.
Use curly brackets instead of square brackets. A set is faster to search, and the output stays the same.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for one change that makes her line better. And she adds: the output must stay exactly the same.
The AI suggests curly brackets, because a set is faster to search. It promises the same output.

visual.heading: Testing the suggestion
visual.hidden_text: Predict the results before they appear.

segments.say: Asha does not trust it yet. Line 12 now has curly brackets, with no colon. She runs every case.

after.say: No. Every case fails. Curly brackets made a set, and a set is never equal to a list. Set, with empty round brackets, is an empty set.
And look at the same-price case: the two equal prices merged into one. A set keeps each value once.
The AI broke her rule: the output did not stay the same. Asha keeps her square brackets.

visual.question: An AI rewrote your loop as one line. How do you prove the output stayed the same?
options: Run both on the same test cases.
Ask the AI if the output is the same.
Check that the new code is shorter.
visual.explain: Only a real run on the same cases proves it. The AI's promise is not proof.

segments.say: Quick check. An AI rewrote your loop as one line. How do you prove the output stayed the same?

after.say: A. Run both versions on the same test cases, and compare every line. A promise is not proof.

items: Plan, write, generate, test, debug, improve.
Run every case again after a fix.
A promise is not proof. A run is.

segments.say: Breather. Asha kept a checklist, ran three cases, and caught two AI mistakes: a missing filter, and curly brackets. Next, the comprehension mistakes beginners make.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 calls back to the AI's curly brackets. Mistake 2 is a spot-it question on step 5. Mistake 3 teaches that print gives back None, then asks. Mistake 4 calls back to Chapter 2's float error.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: curly brackets instead of square

segments.say: Mistake 1 is the AI's improvement. Curly brackets with no colon make a set comprehension. Line 4 shows the type: set.
A set has no fixed order, so line 5 prints it sorted. There is no error. But the list had 3.5 twice, and the set kept 3.85 only once: 3 items instead of 4.
The fix: square brackets for a list. Curly brackets with key, colon, value for a dictionary.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the answer appears.

segments.say: Now you try. Look closely at line 3, and remember step 5.

after.say: A filter at the end cannot have an else. Python stops with a syntax error on line 3.
after.heading: Mistake 2: else after a filter

after.say: The fix: to choose a value for every item, move the if and else to the start. To filter, remove the else.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: a comprehension only to print
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Mistake 3. Print shows text on the screen, but it gives back nothing. Python calls that nothing None.
Line 3 builds a list from three calls to print. Line 4 prints that list.

after.say: None, None, None. The names were printed, but the list is useless.
The fix: when the job is printing, use a normal for loop.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: forgetting to round

segments.say: Mistake 4. Line 3 adds tax with no round. Remember Chapter 2: some floats are stored with a tiny error.
The fix: round inside the comprehension, as line 5 does. Or format the price with two decimal places when you print it.

items: Square brackets for a list.
No `else` after a filter.
Use a loop to print.

segments.say: Last breather. Now you know the four comprehension mistakes that catch most beginners.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.direction: Each recap point appears as it is spoken, then a final quick check, then the badge.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A list comprehension: the new value, then `for`, then an optional `if`.
An `if` at the end filters. `if ... else` at the start chooses a value for every item.
`{key: value for ...}` builds a dictionary. Curly brackets without a colon build a set.
A comprehension makes a new collection. The old one does not change.
Use a normal loop for several steps, a `print()` or a running total.
Refactor with AI, then run both versions on the same cases.

segments.say: Let's recap. A list comprehension: the new value, then for, then an optional if.
An if at the end filters. An if and else at the start chooses a value for every item.
Curly brackets with a colon build a dictionary. And the old collection never changes.
Use a loop for several steps, and with AI, run both versions on the same cases.

visual.question: What does `[n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3] if n > 1]` give?
visual.explain: The filter keeps 2 and 3. The new value doubles each one.

segments.say: One last check. What does this comprehension give?

after.say: D. 4 and 6. The filter keeps 2 and 3, and the new value doubles each one.
